newsitem.title: USA: GM tells Ohio workers parts plants need to improve.
newsitem.headline: GM tells Ohio workers parts plants need to improve.

text.p: Faced with growing competition in the brake systems and suspension business, General Motors Corp. has put four Ohio parts plants on notice that they need to improve their profitability.
GM spokesman James Hagedon said Wednesday the automaker was holding meetings with employees at the plants to devise a plan for improving their operations.
He said there are no plans to shutter the facilities, which employ about 6,500 hourly and salaried workers. But he said GM needed to find a way to operate the facilities profitably.
"You can't keep running plants without making money," he said. "We need a credible plan in a pretty short time frame."

Workers from two of the plants struck Detroit's No. 1 automaker in March 1996 in a dispute over GM's plans to send brake work to less expensive outside parts suppliers. The walkout crippled GM's North American production and ended up costing the automaker $900 million. As part of the settlement, GM agreed to keep the brake work in-house.
GM is facing increasingly stiff competition from other companies in the brake systems and shock-absorber business, said Hagedon.
"We've told people that these businesses have been threatened, but what we've said recently is the gap is growing," said Hagedon, who declined to provide specifics about how uncompetitive GM is.
In addition to talking to employees, GM is investing in the plants and working with suppliers and others to make the businesses more efficient, he said.
"The thing we need to remember here is we're concentrating right now on fixing this," he said.

The two brake plants, located in Dayton, Ohio, employ about 3,500 salaried and hourly workers. The two other facilities are located in nearby Kettering, Ohio. They make suspension components and employ 3,000 workers.

All the units are part of GM's Delphi Chassis Systems, which is under the umbrella of the Delphi Automotive Systems unit. Delphi President J.T. Battenberg, who attended an Economic Club of Detroit luncheon Wednesday, declined to comment on the issue.

Officials of the United Auto Workers Local 696, which represents the Dayton brake workers, could not be reached for comment. Officials from the International Union of Electronic Workers Local 755 also could not be reached. The union represents the Kettering workers.
